problems.description: get_db() resolves the path via g.get("db_path", DATABASE), but db_path is only set by a before_request hook from app.config; any pre-request or outside-context access silently falls back to the module-global DATABASE rather than the configured per-app path, an unnecessary indirection that the later repository refactor (Session 4) will need to unwind.
init_db() does not wrap conn.execute(SCHEMA) in try/finally, so a failed schema creation leaks the connection; low impact for this scale but inconsistent with the teardown discipline used elsewhere.

Flagged discrepancy: the sole convention violation attributable to this commit (task_api.py: 'Classes should use PascalCase') is a false positive — the AST diff measures +0 classes and the flag is triggered by the 'Task: (int, auto)' model line in the module docstring.

strengths: Faithful, complete implementation of the Session 1 spec: all four endpoints, SQLite schema init on startup, JSON error contract (400 for missing title, 404 for missing task), exactly as specified.

Application-factory pattern (create_app) with per-app DATABASE config gives clean test isolation and is well positioned for the Session 2 JWT, Session 3 Celery, and Session 4 repository-refactor sessions.
Parameterized SQL throughout and no string concatenation of user input — no injection surface; sensible VALID_STATUSES whitelist.
Comprehensive pytest suite (207 lines) covering success paths, every validation failure branch, list ordering by created_at desc, and whitespace stripping.
Snake_case functions, module docstring, and timezone-aware created_at timestamps conform to the project's own conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, spec-faithful greenfield Session 1 that introduces no technical debt; the measured 0.73 convention score is misleading since 8 of 9 violations live in pre-existing untouched files and the one new-file flag is a docstring false positive (AST diff shows +0 classes).

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +16 (measured): the inline email-owner lookup + try/except + status-transition guard inside the PUT handler could be extracted into a helper, e.g. _notify_owner_completion(task_id), to keep the endpoint handler flat.

Notification is queued with a snapshot of updated['title'] rather than task_id, so a later title rename leaves a stale email payload; passing the task id and resolving the title in the worker would be more robust.

Convention score 0.73; 9 lint flags (module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE in celery_app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py; PascalCase on app/config instances). Most are false positives — lowercase broker_url/result_backend is idiomatic Celery config and Celery/Flask app objects are instances, not classes — but the measured score should be acknowledged.
Broker/result backend hardcode redis://localhost:6379/0 as default and no retry/backoff policy is set on the Celery task; acceptable for a demo app but noted as a deployment assumption.

strengths: Respects the existing migration pattern: _migrate_add_email mirrors _migrate_add_owner_id and is wired into init_db consistently.
Notification failure is isolated via try/except around .delay(), so a Redis outage never blocks or fails the API response (fire-and-forget matches the documented contract).
Comprehensive tests via monkeypatched .delay cover transition-to-completed, non-completed transitions, title-only updates, and the no-retrigger case.
Config uses env-var overrides with sane defaults, and task_routes routes to a dedicated notifications queue.
Idempotency guard: only fires when status actually transitions to completed, not on repeated PUTs.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested session-3 integration that adds async completion notifications via Celery while faithfully following the codebase's migration, config, and test conventions — the only real debit is the +16 cognitive complexity from inline handler logic, and most of the 9 convention flags are false positives on idiomatic Celery/Flask naming.

problems.description: BaseRepository.table_name is declared as an abstract @property on the ABC, but both subclasses override it with a plain class attribute. It works at runtime but is an inconsistent ABC usage.
The new 81-line repository layer ships with no direct unit tests; correctness rests solely on the existing route-level tests.
BaseRepository.update() would emit invalid SQL ("SET  WHERE") if ever called with zero fields; no current caller triggers it, but a guard/assert would harden it.
Table and column names are interpolated into SQL via f-strings. Safe today because they derive from code constants, not user input, but parameterized schema handling would remove the footgun.

strengths: Behavior-preserving refactor that extracts duplicated raw SQL from six route handlers into a single repository layer
Domain ownership rules (get_by_id_and_owner, list_by_owner) are centralized instead of scattered across routes
New code follows conventions: PascalCase classes, snake_case methods, and adds zero SonarQube bugs/smells/complexity/duplication
Respects the existing Flask patterns: per-request get_db() connections and g.current_user_id scoping are unchanged
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, behavior-preserving repository-layer refactor that reduces duplication and centralizes ownership queries — the 0.73 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py), not new code, and the listed 9 vs. 8 violations are a measurement-count mismatch.

problems.description: list_by_owner_page returns a None sentinel for an invalid cursor instead of raising or returning an empty list, which is inconsistent with sibling repository methods that always return fetchall() results; error semantics are split awkwardly between the repo and the endpoint.
count_by_owner issues a COUNT(*) query on every paginated request even though 'total' is not needed for cursor navigation; could be omitted or made optional for large datasets.

rate_limit_key re-implements JWT decoding from decode_token/require_auth and silently falls back to the client-IP bucket on any invalid token, duplicating auth parsing logic that could drift from the canonical require_auth path.

Flask-Limiter requires injecting a fakeredis storage_uri into create_app in every test path; if a test forgets the injection it silently hits the local Redis default (redis://localhost:6379/0), creating a latent environment dependency.

strengths: Keyset (cursor) pagination uses the same (created_at DESC, id DESC) tiebreak as the existing list_by_owner, giving stable ordering under inserts.
limit+1 over-fetch trick avoids an extra existence query for has_more and correctly caps next_cursor.
Rate limiting is keyed by the authenticated JWT subject with a clean IP fallback for /auth/* and unauthenticated requests.
Tests use fakeredis instead of real Redis, keeping tests hermetic.
Follows existing repository/endpoint patterns, validates query params with proper 400 responses, and keeps the updated API docstring in sync.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted, pattern-respecting feature commit (cursor pagination + user/IP-keyed rate limiting) whose 0.73 convention score reflects mostly pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py), while the new code itself is clean and idiomatic; the measured +1 smell and +41 cognitive complexity stem from the moderate nested logic in list_tasks and rate_limit_key.

compounding_issues: The session-2 JWT/ownership migration (owner_id + ALTER TABLE + legacy compat user) embedded durable schema-migration complexity that every later session had to carry through init_db, and its ad-hoc nature only got cleaned up in the session-4 repository refactor.
Session 5 changed GET /tasks from returning a bare JSON array to an envelope {data, next_cursor, total}, silently breaking the response contract established in sessions 1-4.
Session 5's keyset pagination switched task ordering from created_at DESC (sessions 1-4) to id DESC, a subtle behavior change not called out as such.
key_decisions: JWT auth plus per-user ownership scoping (owner_id) introduced in session 2, which became the security backbone every subsequent data access obeys.
The 'legacy' compatibility user migration in session 2 preserved pre-auth tasks instead of wiping data — a data-continuity decision that later sessions depended on.
Session 4's repository-pattern extraction (TaskRepository/UserRepository) slimmed app.py by ~70 lines and created the seam session 5's pagination and rate limiting build on cleanly.
Celery-based async completion notifications in session 3 exposed a testable delay() seam that sessions 4-5 kept working via monkeypatch.
Session 5's cursor/keyset pagination over id with limit+1 lookahead for O(1) page fetches and a total count.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose steadily and stayed high across all five sessions. Session 1 hardened the seed with input-validation, 404 handling, and timezone fixes (3 passing tests); session 2 delivered a substantial JWT auth + ownership feature with a careful data migration (4 tests); session 3 added a clean Celery-based async notification behind a testable seam (6 tests); session 4 was a disciplined, behavior-preserving refactor into a repository layer with unchanged test count (6 tests); session 5 layered on rate limiting and cursor pagination with thorough coverage (9 tests). Every commit was green, and test count grew monotonically, but the arc shows a slight late-carelessness about API stability — the list endpoint's response shape and ordering changed in the final session.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, well-tested five-session arc — hardening, auth+ownership, async integration, clean repository refactor, then cross-cutting rate limiting/pagination — that improved steadily with every commit green, marred only by late API-contract churn (list response shape and ordering changes).
